127	   For a simple object-oriented language with multiple inheritance, Allen et al. [2008, 2007] and
128	Kim and Ryu [2011] presented three overloading rules: Exclusion Rule, Subtype Rule, and Meet
129	Rule. Every pair of method declarations with the same name must satisfy one of these overloading
130	rules. The authors proved that a set of overloaded method declarations satisfying the overloading
131	rules does not produce any ambiguous method invocation at run time.
132	   To understand the interplay between symmetric multiple dispatch and parametric polymorphism,
133	Allen et al. [2011] focused on a type system without any specific target language and informally
134	presented three other overloading rules: a No Duplicates Rule, a revised Meet Rule, and a Return
135	Type Rule, where every pair of method declarations with the same name must satisfy all three
136	overloading rules. The authors showed that interpreting a polymorphic method declaration as a set
137	of infinitely many monomorphic declarations is not appropriate for overloading resolution. Instead,
138	they considered a polymorphic method declaration as a single declaration whose domain type is
139	existentially quantified over its type parameters as proposed by Bourdoncle and Merz [1997].
140	   In this paper, we present a formal core calculus FGFV (Featherweight Generic Fortress with Vari-
141	ance) for an object-oriented language with symmetric multiple dispatch, multiple inheritance, and
142	parametric polymorphism with variance. For conciseness, FGFV omits functional methods [Allen
143	et al. 2007] and declarations of closed types [Allen et al. 2011], but these could be added back to
144	FGFV in an obvious way. Unlike the prior work, we formally present overloading rules for FGFV,
145	define its dynamic semantics with a novel dynamic dispatch algorithm, and prove type soundness.
146	As we discuss in Section 5.4, defining a provable system for an object-oriented language with
147	asymmetric features requires careful tradeoffs between static expressivity and dynamic efficiency.
148	   In the rest of the paper, we first describe the previous efforts in more detail with concrete
149	code examples (Section 2). After presenting the FGFV calculus that represents an object-oriented

162	In this section, we first discuss existing research achievements in the pursuit of formally defining
163	object-oriented languages with symmetric multiple dispatch, multiple inheritance, and parametric
164	polymorphism with variance. Then, we present how FGFV completes the long-standing endeavor
165	by defining a core calculus with static overloading rules and a dynamic dispatch algorithm that are

168	2.1 Overloading Rules for Multiple Inheritance
169	As we discussed in Section 1, both symmetric multiple dispatch and multiple inheritance may cause
170	ambiguous method calls that cannot be resolved at run time. Let us assume that class C is the only
171	subtype of both classes A and B, and they are all distinct throughout this section. Consider the
172	following overloaded method declarations of m 1 :
173	                    m 1 (x: B, y: C): B = · · ·               m 1 (x: C, y: B): B = · · ·
174	which have the same return type B but different domain types (B, C) and (C, B). For a method
175	invocation m 1 (c, c) where the run-time type of c is C, it is ambiguous which declaration to invoke
176	due to symmetric multiple dispatch: both method declarations are applicable to (c, c) since both
177	(B, C) and (C, B) are supertypes of (C, C), and neither declaration is more specific than the other.
178	Also, consider the following overloaded declarations of m 2 :
179	                    m 2 (x: A):Boolean = · · ·                m 2 (x: B):Boolean = · · ·
180	which have domain types A and B, respectively. For a method invocation m 2 (c), it is ambiguous
181	which declaration to invoke due to multiple inheritance: both declarations are applicable to c and
182	neither declaration is more specific than the other.
183	   In order to guarantee that no such ambiguous method calls are possible at run time, researchers
184	have proposed several calculi with restrictions on overloaded method declarations. CF [Allen et al.
185	2007], Core Fortress, is a core calculus of the Fortress programming language [Allen et al. 2008],
186	which contains components, top-level functions, functional methods, and declarations of exclusive
187	types in addition to multiple inheritance. However, it does not specify the language semantics and
188	informally provides rules for valid overloaded method declarations. FFMM [Kim and Ryu 2011],
189	Featherweight Fortress with Multiple Dispatch and Multiple Inheritance, simplified CF to focus only
190	on multiple inheritance, and it has a complete formalization of the language semantics including
191	overloading rules and its type soundness proof in Coq. Since the overloading rules of CF and FFMM
192	are the same, we will refer to these two languages collectively as Featherweight Fortress (FF).
193	   The overloading rules of FF require every pair in a set of overloaded method declarations to
194	satisfy one of the following rules:
195	    Exclusion Rule: Their domain types are exclusive (their intersection is Bottom, where the
196	       Bottom type is a subtype of every type and no value belongs to Bottom).
197	    Subtype Rule: The domain type of one declaration is a strict subtype of the domain type of
198	       the other, and the return type of the former is a subtype of the return type of the latter.
199	    Meet Rule: The domain types are not exclusive nor in a subtype relation, and the overloaded
200	       set contains a third disambiguating method declaration which we call the meet of the pair.
201	       The meet of two method declarations is more specific than each of the declarations and less
202	       specific than any other method declaration that is more specific than both declarations.

232	2.2   Overloading Rules for Multiple Inheritance and Generics
233	Similarly for multiple inheritance, generics may cause ambiguous method calls that cannot be
234	resolved at run time. Consider the following overloaded declarations of sort:

239	Their domain types are respectively łListI JP K where P is a subtype of Až and łListI JP K where P
240	is a subtype of Bž; for a method invocation sort(l) where the run-time type of l is ListI JC K, both
241	declarations are applicable to l and neither declaration is more specific than the other.
242	   In order to support generics as well for symmetric multiple dispatch, Allen et al. [2011] proposed
243	new overloading rules for given generic declarations of types and methods. Even though they
244	did not present a specific language with generics, we refer to the underlying language as FGF,
245	Featherweight Generic Fortress. To support generics, the authors re-defined the terms applicability
246	and specificity for generic method declarations and their overloading rules. A generic method
247	declaration d is applicable to a type α if there exists an instance D of d that is applicable to α, that
248	is, the domain type of D is a supertype of α. For example, consider the following generic method
249	declaration:
250	                                          mJP <: AK(x: P): P = · · ·
251	which has one type parameter P with an upper bound A. It is applicable to Bottom, C, and A, because
252	they are subtypes of A. In general, a generic method declaration d 1 is more specific than d 2 if the
253	applicable set of d 1 is a subset of that of d 2 , where the applicable set of a method declaration is a set
254	of types to which the declaration is applicable. Note that a monomorphic method declaration is a
255	generic method declaration without any type parameter.
256	   The overloading rules of FGF require every pair in a set of overloaded method declarations to
257	satisfy all of the following rules as illustrated in Figure 1:

263	       must be some argument type α for which one method is applicable and the other is not).
264	    Meet Rule: Let S be the intersection of the applicable sets of the two method declarations; if
265	       S is not empty, then the overloaded set must contain a method declaration (not necessarily
266	       distinct from the two given method declarations) whose applicable set is precisely S.
267	    Return Type Rule: If one method declaration d 1 is more specific than d 2 , for any non-Bottom
268	       type α in the applicable set of d 1 , the return type of an instance of d 2 that is applicable to α

286	declarations. Meet Rule plays an important role for ensuring the existence of a disambiguating

289	2.3    Overloading Rules for Multiple Inheritance and Generics with Variance
290	Variance, as well as symmetric multiple dispatch, multiple inheritance, and generics, may cause
291	ambiguous method calls that cannot be resolved at run time. We revisit the ambiguous sort example
292	in Section 2.2. This time, we define the same method in a simpler way using covariant definitions
293	of ListC and SortedListC . Consider the following overloaded method declarations of sort:
294	                              d1 :       sort(x: ListC JAK): SortedListC JAK = · · ·
295	                              d2 :       sort(x: ListC JB K): SortedListC JB K = · · ·
296	Similarly to the example in Section 2.2, for a method invocation sort(l) where the run-time type of
297	l is ListC JC K, it is ambiguous which declaration to invoke: both d 1 and d 2 are applicable to l and
298	neither is more specific than the other. In order to ensure that there is no ambiguous method calls
299	for sort at run time, we need to add a disambiguating method declaration d 3 :
300	                              d3 :       sort(x: ListC JC K): SortedListC JC K = · · ·
301	with a more specific return type than those of d 1 and d 2 for type preservation.
302	   Variance also adds complications in type-sound dynamic dispatch. Let us now assume that ListC
303	is covariant in its type argument but SortedListI is invariant. Then, the set of three method
304	declarations above replacing SortedListC with SortedListI would be invalid, because the return
305	type SortedListI JAK of d 1 would not be a supertype of the return type SortedListI JC K of d 3 .

310	  Supporting variance in a type-sound manner requires keeping track of the static types of method
311	invocations at run time. Let us again assume that ListC is covariant but SortedListI is invariant,
312	and consider the following overloaded set (note that d 3 now has a type parameter P):
313	                            d1 :             sort(x: ListC JAK): SortedListI JAK = · · ·
314	                            d2 :             sort(x: ListC JB K): SortedListI JB K = · · ·
315	                            d3 :         sortJP K(x: ListC JC K): SortedListI JP K = · · ·
316	as well as the following generic method declaration of merge:
317	            mergeJP K(x: SortedListI JP K, y: SortedListI JP K): SortedListI JP K = · · ·
318	For a method invocation merge(sort(l 1 ), sort(l 2 )) where the static types of l 1 and l 2 are both ListC JAK
319	and their run-time types are ListC JAK and ListC JC K, respectively, at compile time, both method
320	invocations sort(l 1 ) and sort(l 2 ) choose d 1 and their static types are both SortedListI JAK. Thus,
321	the above merge call statically invokes the following instance of the generic merge declaration:
322	                  merge(x: SortedListI JAK, y: SortedListI JAK): SortedListI JAK
323	that is applicable to (SortedListI JAK, SortedListI JAK). However, at run time, while sort(l 1 )
324	chooses d 1 and its return type is SortedListI JAK, sort(l 2 ) chooses d 3 and its return type depends
325	on what actual type is inferred at run time for the type parameter P. If the dynamic type inference
326	algorithm instantiates P as A, sort(l 2 ) has type SortedListI JAK, which is type sound. But it could
327	equally plausibly instantiate P as some other type T , and then no dynamic instance of the generic
328	merge declaration would be applicable to (SortedListI JAK, SortedListI JT K). Hence, the merge
329	call would fail, despite the fact that the program successfully passed static type checking. In order to
330	help run-time type inference algorithms make type-sound choices of type arguments, the language
331	semantics needs to make the static types of method invocations available at run time.
332	   In this paper, we present FGFV, which sheds light on the long-standing endeavor to support
333	strong types, symmetric multiple dispatch, multiple inheritance, and parametric polymorphism with
334	variance. We formalize the static overloading rules for FGFV using existential types and universal
335	types quantified over method type parameters, and design a new dynamic dispatch algorithm that
336	is proven type-sound to guarantee unambiguous method calls and type preservation at run time.

598	Now, we formalize the overloading rules informally discussed in Section 2.2 for FGFV.
599	
600	4.1     Formalization of Overloading Rules
601	The overloading rules require that every pair in a set of overloaded method declarations satisfies all
602	three rules defined in Figure 5. To determine whether one method declaration is more specific than
603	the other, while the informal rules in Section 2.2 used the subset relation of their applicable sets,
604	which is not practically checkable, we use the subtype relation of their domain types as in Allen
605	et al. [2011]. Note that even though FGFV additionally supports variance annotations of trait type
606	parameters, the overloading rules for FGF remain the same because covariant or contravariant types
607	affect only the well-formedness of method declarations rather than the validity of overloading.
608	   If two method declarations have different names, they vacuously satisfy all the rules ([No-Dup-
609	Triv], [Meet-Triv], and [Return-Triv]). The No Duplicates Rule also checks whether the domain
610	types of two declarations are different; if the domain type of one declaration is not a subtype of the
611	domain type of the other, they satisfy the rule ([No-Dup-Not-Less] and [No-Dup-Not-Gtr]). The
612	Meet Rule is satisfied if two domain types exclude each other ([Meet-Excl]), they are in a subtype
613	relation ([Meet-Less] and [Meet-Gtr]), or the domain type of a third declaration of the same
614	name is the intersection type of the domain types of two declarations ([Meet-Third]). The Return
615	Type Rule is satisfied if two domain types are not in a subtype relation ([Return-Not-Less]), or if
616	two arrow types derived from the two declarations are in a subtype relation ([Return-Test]).

781	4.3   Unique Existence of the Most Specific Declaration
782	  Theorem 4.1. For any method invocation, there always exists a unique most specific method
783	declaration in its set of applicable method declarations.
784	   Proof Sketch. We first show that the more specific relation of method declarations is a partial
785	order. It is clearly reflexive and transitive since the existential subtype relation is reflexive and
786	transitive. The No Duplicates Rule guarantees that it is antisymmetric. Under the partial order, a
787	set of applicable method declarations is a meet semilattice. The Meet Rule guarantees the existence
788	of a meet for every nonempty subset of the set. Proving the existence of the most specific method
789	declaration is straightforward by structural induction on the meet semilattice.                     □

996	5.2.3 Solving the Bounds.
997	   The last step of the dispatch semipredicate is to solve the computed type bounds for method type
998	parameters as in Figure 10. The solve rules compute a valid substitution σ for all the method type
999	parameters in K , which satisfies the declared bounds in K and the computed bounds from type
1000	matching ⟨l ⟩ and ⟨u ⟩ . The solving step succeeds if any of the type bounds leads to a valid
1001	substitution. For declared type bounds for method type parameters P , P ′ and their computed type
1002	bounds ⟨l , l ′⟩ and ⟨u , u ′⟩ from type matching, rule [Solve-Step] nondeterministically selects
1003	i-th type bounds ⟨l i , li′⟩ and ⟨u i , ui′⟩ that successfully compute a valid substitution. Starting from
1004	the rightmost type parameter P ′, the rule computes a substitution [д ′/P ′] by taking the intersection
1005	of the upper bounds of P ′. Because д ′ is a ground type, the solving step never instantiates method
1006	type parameters with Bottom. The match premises propagate the choice of д ′ for P ′ to the declared
1007	lower bounds of P ′ to collect additional constraints on P . Then, the rule combines the additional
1008	constraints and the originally computed bounds, and inductively solves the combined bounds to
1009	compute the substitution [д/P ]. From this, it produces a valid substitution [д/P , д ′/P ′].
1010	   Note that the rule selects i-th type bounds nondeterministically while it checks type parameters
1011	deterministically from the rightmost one. Because the scope of a well-formed method type parameter
1012	extends to the right and method type parameters can appear only in lower bounds, for well-formed
1013	type parameters { χ } <: P <: {η }, the upper bounds {η } do not contain any of P , and P j does
1014	not appear in the lower bounds of Pi for i ≤ j. Thus, the choice of дi for Pi does not affect the
1015	upper bounds of P j , which allows us to compute a substitution in the right-to-left order by taking
1016	intersections of upper bounds. Since the choice of дj for P j may place additional constraints on Pi ’s

1221	5.4     Discussion
1222	Defining a provable system for an object-oriented language requires addressing various technical
1223	challenges due to the structural asymmetries inherent in the language design. One can have a
1224	variable of type Any, but one cannot have a variable of type Bottom. The ilk of an actual argument
1225	must be a subtype, not a supertype, of the method’s parameter type. The ilk of a returned value
1226	must be a subtype, not a supertype, of the method’s return type. A trait may declare ancestors but
1227	not descendants. Such asymmetries prohibit seemingly symmetric features from being treated as
1228	duals. One might think at first glance that upper bounds and lower bounds of type parameters
1229	should be related symmetrically (perhaps treated as duals), but they cannot be.
1230	   For example, the łAncestor Meet Rulež (expressed in this paper by rule [Anc-Same-Trait]) was
1231	introduced into Fortress in 2012 by Guy Steele and David Chase [Steele and Chase 2012] to design
1232	an expressive type system with union and intersection types. This rule permits proofs that (a) if
1233	T JP K is covariant in P then T J(α ⊓ α ′)K ≡ (T Jα K ⊓ T Jα ′ K), and (b) if T JP K is contravariant in P
1234	then T J(α ⊔ α ′)K ≡ (T Jα K ⊓ T Jα ′ K) (that last set operator is indeed ⊓, not ⊔). These equivalences
1235	allow simplification of type expressions by moving type union and type intersection operators
1236	out of type arguments. However, the łobvious other two casesž are not available. When T JP K is
1237	covariant in P, T J(α ⊔ α ′)K is not equivalent to some simple combination of T Jα K and T Jα ′ K; the
1238	best one can say is that (T Jα K ⊔ T Jα ′ K) <: T J(α ⊔ α ′)K.
1239	   In 2012, the developers of Fortress explored an alternate set of language restrictions that exploited
1240	these asymmetries to ensure that exponential blowup could occur at run time only when union
1241	types interacted with contravariance (the dual case of intersection types interacting with covariance
1242	could not occur). They then contemplated two alternatives for avoiding the exponential blowup.
1243	One possibility is to eliminate contravariant type parameters and contravariant type relationships.
1244	This has the consequence that arrow types must be treated as invariant, rather than contravariant,
1245	in the type to the left of the arrow. This could make it inconvenient to use higher-order functions
1246	such as map, but one can compensate by introducing rules of coercion, so that if a function of type
1247	(α → ρ) is used in a situation where a function of type (α ′ → ρ ′) is required, it can be coerced to a
1248	new function object if α ′ <: α and ρ <: ρ ′. The other possibility is to eliminate union types from the
1249	type theory; this might require restricting the language so that, for example, in an if-then-else
1250	expression, the type of the then subexpression must be either a supertype or a subtype of the else
1251	subexpression. Alternatively, some sort of pseudo-join (least common existing supertype) operation
1252	could be used. One could go even further, also eliminating intersection types from the type theory
1253	by further restricting the language and possibly using a pseudo-meet operation.
1254	   We carefully designed our dynamic dispatch algorithm to make a balanced tradeoff between static
1255	expressivity and dynamic efficiency. We accept the potential for exponential blowup because we
1256	believe that such cases are unlikely to arise in practice and the use of union and intersection types
1257	in the type theory, even if not directly expressible by the programmer, makes the language more
1258	expressive. Also, while one could in principle allow any lower bound to refer to any type parameter,
1259	dynamic overloading resolution would then have to solve a general set of type inequalities, requiring
1260	a complex technique with multiple iterations; we chose instead to impose left-to-right scoping
1261	on method type parameters, allowing use of a simple, one-pass right-to-left scan. We believe this
1262	tradeoff represents a relatively small sacrifice of expressivity for a large gain in dynamic efficiency.
1263	   Dynamically inferring type instantiations can incur run-time overhead. In simple invariant cases,
1264	we expect the run-time cost to be relatively low but nonzero. For example, if we pass a value of type
1265	ListJStringK to a method such as fooJT K(x:ListJT K), T is matched only once and no union

1274	   The biggest challenge we faced in trying to find a provable system was grappling with the
1275	language asymmetries described above and trying to understand their consequences. In particular,
1276	the Fortress team had assumed, because it seemed from several working examples to be in accord
1277	with intuition, that once the tightest possible upper and lower bounds for a method type parameter
1278	have been found, then the union (or pseudo-union) of the lower bounds should be chosen as the
1279	type to be used for that type parameter. We considered this and the hybrid technique of using the
1280	intersection of upper bounds only when the union of lower bounds is Bottom, but we were unable
1281	to complete the proofs of correctness of both the techniques. Since the minimum requirement for a
1282	type to instantiate a method type parameter is that it satisfies all the lower and upper bounds of the
1283	type parameter, the dynamic dispatch algorithm presented here always chooses the intersection of
1284	the upper bounds.
1285	   In the work presented here, as in previous work, one of the most difficult parts is finding the
1286	necessary substitution σ to satisfy the rule [E-Sub] for existential subtyping during static analysis.
1287	This is more difficult than the corresponding calculation during dynamic dispatch because at run
1288	time one always matches an ilk (which contains no type parameters) to a type, but at compile time
1289	one must match a type against a type, where each type may contain type parameters. Indeed, we do
1290	not present a specific static type inference algorithm that finds the substitution σ in rule [E-Sub],
1291	but only refer to previous work in this area. However, we conjecture that the match rule presented
1292	here can serve this role after being extended to handle the case of matching two type parameters.

1296	dynamic dispatch algorithm. Allen et al. proposed rules for defining overloaded functions that
1297	ensure type safety under symmetric multiple dispatch in an object-oriented language with multiple
1298	inheritance, and showed how to check the rules without requiring the entire type hierarchy. They

1299	proposed the overloading rules in the context of a set of class declarations and function declarations
1300	without defining a language with complete static and dynamic semantics. Therefore, their work
1301	does not guarantee that the static overloading rules and the way a language chooses a method to
1302	invoke at run time match correctly. While FGFV does not support features like modularity, nominal
1303	exclusion, and closed types in their work, they can be added in an obvious way. As the related work
1304	section of Allen et al. [2011] discusses in detail, most earlier systems like Dubious [Millstein and
1305	Chambers 1999, 2002; Millstein 2003], MultiJava [Clifton et al. 2006], and F(EML) [Lee and Chambers
1306	2006] supported overloading with symmetric multiple dynamic dispatch with multiple inheritance,
1307	but without support for polymorphic methods or types. While ML ≤ [Bourdoncle and Merz 1997]
1308	integrates polymorphism and symmetric multiple dynamic dispatch, it lacks multiple inheritance.
1309	   ParaSail [Taft 2011, 2016] is a parallel programming language designed to support inherently safe
1310	and secure, highly parallel applications. It also constrains the scope of type parameters, prohibiting
1311	a bound on a type parameter from referring to type parameter bindings to its left, so that dynamic
1312	type inference can be fast. However, ParaSail does not support covariant and contravariant type
1313	parameters, and it does not provide any formal specification.
1314	   Julia [Bezanson et al. 2015, 2017] is a dynamic programming language with symmetric multiple
1315	dispatch. It provides a type declaration and type annotation sublanguage, but does not have a static
1316	type system. Thus, it does not check the validity of overloaded methods, and only uses the subtype
1317	relation to find the most specific method among overloaded methods at run time.

1343	7 CONCLUSION
1344	We defined FGFV, a core calculus for an object-oriented language with symmetric multiple dispatch,
1345	multiple inheritance, and parametric polymorphism with variance. In order to ensure type soundness
1346	of FGFV, it must guarantee no ambiguous method invocations at run time, and preserve type even
1347	when a method invocation is dispatched to a different method at run time from the method chosen
1348	at compile time. Thus, we formalized overloading rules using existential types and universal types
1349	quantified over method type parameters to mechanically check whether overloaded polymorphic
1350	methods are valid. As a result, in a well-formed program that satisfies the overloading rules, there
1351	always exists the single most specific method to invoke with respect to both static argument types
1352	and dynamic argument types. Further, with the static types of method invocation expressions
1353	delivered to run time, the dynamic semantics of FGFV that uses the new dynamic dispatch algorithm
1354	we presented is proven to make type-sound choices among applicable method declarations.
